catalog_quote: Tlapanec employs iambic feet aligned to the right edge of the prosodic word (Marlett and Weathers 2018: 23; Suárez 1983: 26). The acoustic correlate of accent in Tlapanec is still unclear. On the one hand, Marlett and Weathers (2018: 23) state that “it is not clear that something comparable to stress is appropriately identified in Me’phaa”; and speakers also have difficulty in identifying which syllable is ‘strong’. [...] In order to reflect the fact that the acoustic correlate of stress in Tlapanec is still unclear, we refer to syllables as either “weak” versus “strong”, rather than “unstressed” versus “stressed” [...] Marlett and Weathers (2018: 23–24) remark that there is evidence that words and phrases are prosodically right-headed (whether this syllable has a short vowel or long vowel; thus, quantity-insensitive) [...] a vowel can undergo syncope in any syllable except for this strong syllable. Some contrasts are maintained only in the final syllable of the prosodic word; this is the phonological correlate of accent. [p. 100] Tlapanec has been argued to employ quantity-insensitive iambic feet and aligns them at the right edge of the prosodic word, assigned iteratively from right to left (cf. Marlett and Weathers 2018). [...] the strong syllable is indicated with a raised vertical line, while secondary accent is indicated with a lowered vertical line. (19) ni(gi.ˌta)(ʃmá.ˈtaa) ‘he was pulled’
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: The final syllable of the prosodic word is the strong (accented) syllable: quantity-insensitive iambic feet are built from the right edge, and only that syllable licenses contrastive vowel length, nasalization and contour tones. The language is tonal (3 level tones, 9 melodies) and the authors stress that the phonetic correlate of accent is still disputed (no clear stress per Marlett & Weathers 2018; onset-consonant lengthening per Carrasco 2012 and Cornelio Tiburcio 2022; tone-conditioned per Herrera Zendejas 2018).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 100: 'Tlapanec has been argued to employ quantity-insensitive iambic feet and aligns them at the right edge of the prosodic word, assigned iteratively from right to left (cf. Marlett and Weathers 2018).. the strong syllable is indicated with a raised vertical line, while secondary accent is indicated with a lowered vertical line.' Secondary accent on the strong syllable of each non-head foot; the final foot is the head foot. Feet are disyllabic, so stems are mono- or disyllabic and affixed words get iterative feet.
new_statements.exceptions: Acoustic correlate unclear; speakers have difficulty identifying the strong syllable; a few contour tones occur in non-final syllables; Herrera Zendejas 2018 claims a tone-conditioned position instead of fixed final.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain = the prosodic word ('the domain of accentuation, the domain of a minimality requirement, and the domain of some tonal processes', p. 100), i.e. stem plus affixes; compounds may not form one prosodic word (fn. 14). Marlett & Weathers 2018 say words and phrases alike are right-headed.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source's data are from the Huehuetepec variety (community of Zilacayotitlán, mun. Atlamajalcingo del Monte), which Marlett & Weathers 2018 Table 1 place under ISO tcf as 'tlapaneco del este [Huehuetepec]' ([tcf-Zila]); Glottolog mali1285 = tcf, so it is the same language but not the Malinaltepec-town subvariety. The statement is explicitly grounded in Marlett & Weathers 2018 (genus-wide, sampling [tcf-CVil], [tcf-Tepe], [tcf-Zila]) and Suárez 1983:26 (Malinaltepec). The competing tone-conditioned claim (Herrera Zendejas 2018) is about Malinaltepec proper. The instrumental confirmation of final stress (Cornelio Tiburcio 2022) is from Ciénega del Sauce, an Acatepec-type variety (acat1239), not tcf.

new_statements.quote: The prosody of other dialects of Me’phaa has been reported as iambic or at least at word-final (Cline (2013), Herrera Zendejas, personal communication; Marlett, personal communication), therefore the most prominent syllables phonetically should be the final syllable and, possibly, the last syllable of each iamb. [p. 106] [...] In summary, syllable duration and intensity appear to be cues to prominence in Me’phaa Vátháá, whereas frequency and vocalic quality appear not to contribute to distinctions between syllables. Both duration and intensity point to accentual hypotheses that would make Me’phaa Vátháá accent either word-final or iambic. [p. 111]
new_statements.citation: Coto Solano, Rolando. 2017. Tonal Reduction and Literacy in the Me'phaa Vátháá Community. PhD diss., University of Arizona. 317 pp.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: LuaTeX text). extracted text: printed p. 106 opens Sec. 3.5.2 'Prominence' with 'The prosody of other dialects of Me'phaa has been reported as iambic or at least at word-final (Cline (2013), Herrera Zendejas, personal communication; Marlett, per-/sonal communication), therefore the most prominent syllables phonetically should be the final syllable and, possibly, the last syllable of each iamb.' -- verbatim apart from the 'per-' line-break hyphen and the under-macron glyphs that extracted text prints on a separate line. extracted text: printed p. 111 has 'In summary, syllable duration and intensity appear to be cues to prominence in Me'phaa Vátháá, whereas frequency and vocalic quality appea…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (final syllable) and as Uchihara & Tiburcio Cano 2022 (iambic feet, final syllable strong) and Marlett & Weathers 2018 (right-headed). Adds instrumental correlates: duration and intensity mark the final syllable, F0 and vowel quality do not; final syllables admit all 8 tones vs. 5 non-finally. This also refines Uchihara & Tiburcio Cano's remark that the acoustic correlate of accent is 'still unclear'. Describes the Zilacayotitlán (Vátháá / Huehuetepec) subvariety, the same community as Uchihara & Tiburcio Cano 2022.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level prominence falls on the final syllable of the word; the author assumes an iambic / word-final system from the other varieties and tests it instrumentally in Me'phaa Vátháá: final syllables carry all eight tones vs. five in non-final syllables (Table 3.21), are 21% (careful speech) to 46% (reduced speech) longer than non-final syllables (Table 3.22), and are louder than penults and antepenults; F0 and vowel quality do not vary by position. He concludes that the evidence supports either word-final accent or iambic feet.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Possible: 'the last syllable of each iamb' (p. 106); intensity 'provides evidence for an iambic structure' since penult and antepenult both differ from the final syllable and the antepenult is closer to the final in reduced speech (pp. 110-111). Not asserted as a rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None as lexical exceptions. Caveats: the duration and intensity differences are largely neutralized in careful (read) speech and clear only in reduced speech (pp. 110-111); the author calls the understanding of Me'phaa Vátháá prosody 'preliminary' (p. 39); a phonetic-prominence study, not a phonological stress rule, and it does not decide between word-final and iambic.
new_statements.identity_note: Coto Solano 2017 describes Me'phaa Vátháá, 'centered around the town of Zilacayotitlán in the Atlamajalcingo del Monte municipality' and 'sometimes subsumed into Malinaltepec Me'phaa' (p. 24); this is the Huehuetepec/Zilacayotitlán subvariety ([tcf-Zila] in Marlett & Weathers 2018; Glottolog dialect zila1239 under mali1285) and the same speaker community as Uchihara & Tiburcio Cano 2022 and Tiburcio Cano 2017. Duncan 2017 works with speakers from the Iliatenco municipality, 'commonly subsumed under the designation of Malinaltepec Me'phaa' (p. 13), = Cruz La Villa (Iliatenco) [tcf-CVil] in Marlett & Weathers 2018 Table 1, also within mali1285. Neither work covers the Malinaltepec town variety itself.

tone_statements.citation: Uchihara, Hiroto & Gregorio Tiburcio Cano. 2020 [online 20 Sept 2019]. A phonological account of Tlapanec (Mè'phàà) tonal alternation. Journal of Linguistics 56(4): 807-863. Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/S002222671900032X
tone_statements.quote: There are three basic tones: high, mid, and low; mid is the unmarked, default tone. In addition, there can be a combination of two tones on a short vowel and up to four tones on a long vowel. The overwhelmingly general case is that there is only one tone per syllable in monomorphemic forms. Contour tones are (almost always) formed in the morphology, either by compounding or affixation (Weathers and Carrasco 1988: 38). … the underlying tones remain (as does nasalization and usually glottalization) and are relinked to the new segmental material, forming contour tones as necessary.
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones (high, mid, low; mid the unmarked default), normally one per syllable; contours are combinations built in morphology when root tones relink to suffix vowels; long syllable: two TBUs.

tone_statements.citation: Coto Solano, Rolando. 2017. Tonal Reduction and Literacy in the Me'phaa Vátháá Community. PhD diss., University of Arizona. 317 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Tlapanec (Mè’phàà) is known for its enigmatic tonal alternation in verb forms according to person and aspect-mode categories, in addition to suppletion and other segmental alternations. In this paper, we argue that the tonal alternations observed in Tlapanec regular agentive verbs can be straightforwardly accounted for by phonology, without resorting to any extreme abstractness: the lexical tones of the prefixes and the verb stems, with underspecification and floating tones, and cross-linguistically common tone processes such as tone spreading and floating tone docking.

tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone (3 levels H M L per the descriptive literature); verbal person/TAM tonal alternations analysed with floating tones, spreading and docking.

tone_statements.quote: En este trabajo se analizará la relación entre el F0 y la prominencia en la lengua meʔpʰa, variante de Unión de las Peras, Guerrero, donde, a nivel paradigmático, las diferencias en la tonía se concretizan en tres tonos de nivel (A, M, B) y seis tonos de contorno (tres descendentes (A͡M, A͡B, M͡B) y tres ascendentes (M͡A, B͡M, B͡A), así como se muestra en (1). … Más allá de las diferencias distintivas que tiene el F0, el meʔpʰa es un claro ejemplo de lenguas que, siendo tonales, se sirven del F0 para señalar la prominencia de la palabra.
tone_statements.translation: This paper analyses the relation between F0 and prominence in the meʔpʰa language, variety of Unión de las Peras, Guerrero, where, at the paradigmatic level, the differences in tone are realised as three level tones (H, M, L) and six contour tones (three falling (HM, HL, ML) and three rising (MH, LM, LH)), as shown in (1). … Beyond the distinctive differences carried by F0, meʔpʰa is a clear example of languages that, being tonal, use F0 to signal word prominence.
tone_statements.locator: p. 1 (unnumbered), opening paragraph before ex. (1) 'Tonos de nivel y de contorno' and the paragraph after ex. (1)
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones (high, mid, low) and six contours (3 falling, 3 rising); accent iambic or on the highest tone from the right edge, cued by a slight F0 rise; floating low tone marks 3sg possessive.

sources.note: Per Cornelio Tiburcio 2022: 4, Herrera (2018) proposes that the position of the tonic syllable in Me'phaa is conditioned by tone: stress goes to the syllable bearing the higher tone toward the final position (e.g. /ʃjáma/ H-M stresses the H syllable, /àga/ L-M the M syllable); a tone-stress interaction analysis that Cornelio's acoustic study rejects.
